overview.tagline: AI-Powered Pattern-Aware Code Analysis & Developer Education Engine
overview.phase_goal: Validate core hypothesis: developers prefer tools that teach, not just flag. Ship minimal CLI scanning Python files for 5 hard-coded patterns with educational explanations.
success_criteria: CLI runs on any Python file without crashing
Detects all 5 patterns with <5% false positive rate on test corpus
10 developer testers report 'teach' framing more valuable than 'lint' framing
At least 3 testers say they learned something new

patterns.description: List all detectable patterns with descriptions

patterns.overview: 5 hard-coded patterns covering AI-generated code signatures, async bugs, security, and Python idioms

pattern_list.name: generic-exception-swallow
pattern_list.description: Catching broad exceptions and silently ignoring them - a hallmark of LLM-generated code that 'works' but hides bugs
triggers: except Exception: ... (with only logging, no re-raise)

conditions: handler.body contains only Pass, or only logging call

teaching.what: You're catching all exceptions and silently swallowing them.
teaching.why: This hides bugs, masks crashes, and makes debugging nearly impossible. If something fails, you'll never know. LLMs often generate this pattern because it 'prevents errors' in the most superficial way.
teaching.fix: Catch specific exceptions you can handle. Re-raise or log with traceback for unexpected ones.
teaching.spot_it_yourself: Search for 'except Exception' and 'except:' in your codebase. Ask: 'What specific error am I handling here?' If you can't answer, you're probably swallowing bugs.

pattern_list.name: placeholder-code-in-production
pattern_list.description: TODO/FIXME comments paired with placeholder implementations - LLMs generate stubs they never filled in
triggers: Function body is only pass/... after docstring

ast_detection.approach: Two-pass: regex finds TODO/FIXME comments, AST checks if following statement is Pass/Raise NotImplementedError
conditions: Body contains only Pass or Ellipsis (after docstring)

teaching.what: You have placeholder code that was never implemented.
teaching.why: LLMs often generate function stubs with TODO comments, expecting you to fill them in. Shipping these means silent failures or crashes in production. It's also a sign of copy-paste without review.
teaching.fix: Implement the function, remove it if unused, or raise a clear custom exception if intentionally incomplete.
teaching.spot_it_yourself: Run 'grep -rn "TODO\|FIXME" *.py' and check each hit. Is there actual implementation below the comment? Set up pre-commit hooks to catch these.

pattern_list.name: blocking-call-in-async
pattern_list.description: Using blocking calls (time.sleep, requests.get, open()) inside async functions, defeating the purpose of async
triggers: open() for file I/O in async def

conditions: Call matches known blocking function signature

teaching.what: You're using a blocking call inside an async function.
teaching.why: Async functions run on an event loop. Blocking calls freeze the ENTIRE loop, not just your function. If you await asyncio.sleep(1), other tasks run. If you call time.sleep(1), everything stops for a second. This defeats the purpose of async and can cause timeouts, unresponsive servers, and cascading failures.
teaching.fix: Replace blocking calls with their async equivalents: time.sleep → asyncio.sleep, requests → aiohttp/httpx, open → aiofiles.
teaching.spot_it_yourself: In any 'async def', search for: time.sleep, requests., open(, input(. These are red flags. The rule: if you're in async-land, everything I/O-related should be awaited.
teaching.example_bad:
async def fetch_data(url):
    response = requests.get(url)  # Blocks entire event loop!
    time.sleep(1)  # Even worse - freezes everything
    return response.json()
teaching.example_good:
async def fetch_data(url):
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        async with session.get(url) as response:
            await asyncio.sleep(1)  # Other tasks can run
            return await response.json()

pattern_list.name: hardcoded-secret
pattern_list.description: API keys, passwords, tokens, or secrets hardcoded in source files
triggers: String matching API key patterns (sk-*, ghp_*, xoxb-*, etc.)
Private key content (BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY)

value_patterns.name: Generic High Entropy
value_patterns.pattern: String >20 chars with high entropy in sensitive variable

teaching.what: You have a secret (API key, password, token) hardcoded in your source file.
teaching.why: Secrets in code get committed to git, shared in code reviews, and leaked in logs. Once a secret is in git history, it's there forever (unless you rewrite history). Attackers actively scan GitHub for leaked credentials. This is how breaches happen.
teaching.fix: Use environment variables (os.environ['API_KEY']), a .env file (with python-dotenv), or a secrets manager. Never commit real credentials.
teaching.spot_it_yourself: Before every commit, run 'git diff --staged | grep -iE "key|secret|token|password"'. Better: use pre-commit hooks with tools like detect-secrets or gitleaks.
teaching.example_good:
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()

OPENAI_API_KEY = os.environ['OPENAI_API_KEY']
DATABASE_URL = os.environ['DATABASE_URL']

pattern_list.name: mutable-default-argument
pattern_list.description: Using mutable objects (list, dict, set) as default function arguments - a classic Python gotcha

teaching.what: You're using a mutable object (list, dict, set) as a default argument.
teaching.why: Default arguments are evaluated ONCE when the function is defined, not each time it's called. This means all calls share the same list/dict/set object. Modifying it in one call affects all future calls. This is one of Python's most infamous gotchas and catches everyone at least once.
teaching.fix: Use None as default and create the mutable object inside the function.
teaching.spot_it_yourself: In function signatures, look for '=[]', '={}', or '=set()'. These are almost always bugs. The pattern 'param=None' followed by 'if param is None: param = []' is the correct idiom.
teaching.example_bad:
def add_item(item, items=[]):
    items.append(item)
    return items

add_item('a')  # Returns ['a']
add_item('b')  # Returns ['a', 'b'] - Wait, what?!
teaching.example_good:
def add_item(item, items=None):
    if items is None:
        items = []
    items.append(item)
    return items

add_item('a')  # Returns ['a']
add_item('b')  # Returns ['b'] - Correct!

import time
import requests

async def bad_sleep():

    return response.json()

async def good_async():
